Ahirbudhnya Saṁhitā
------------------------------------------
Among the extant Vaiṣṇava आगमस् of the Pāñcarātra school, the Ahirbudhnya Saṁhitā is an important work. ‘Ahir-budhnya’ is one who, in the form of an ‘ahi’ or serpent, is the ‘budhna’ or foundation of the world. So, literally it refers to शेष or अनन्त, the thousand-hooded serpent, on whose head the world is said to be supported, according to the accounts in some of the पुराणस्. It is also mentioned as one of the names of शिव who, according to the Vaiṣṇava scriptures, is a great devotee of विष्णु. In this work he is identified with शिव. ‘Saṁhitā’ is a general name given to any systematically arranged text.
As in the case of many other Hindu religious works, it is rather difficult to assign any date for this work. Otto Schrader feels that it must have been composed later than A. D. 300 (See his Introduction to the Pāñcarātra and the Ahirbudhnya Saṁhitā, Madras: Adyar Library and Research Centre, 1973.)
The Saṁhitā opens with a dialogue between two sages भरद्वाज and दुर्वासस्. भरद्वाज requests दुर्वासस् to propound the mystery of सुदर्शन, the wondrous discus of Lord विष्णु. दुर्वासस् agrees to narrate faithfully the teachings given by Ahirbudhnya (Śiva) to नारद on this subject, but only briefly. The original Saṁhitā before condensation is said to have had 240 chapters. However, the present printed text has 3880 verses in the anuṣṭubh metre, spread over 60 chapters.
The teachings of this work can be briefly summed up as follows: पर-ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, is the highest Truth. He is One, without beginning or end, all-pervading, free from all blemish, full and perfect. He resides in all beings and is called नारायण. His real nature can be experienced only in the state of लिबेरतिओन्, which again is possible only by His grace and not by one’s own efforts.
He has two śaktis or powers: क्रियाशक्ति and bhūtiśakti. The सुदर्शन चक्र is actually the क्रियाशक्ति representing the active side or the energetic aspect of the Lord (chs. 3 and 8 to 12). When it activates the bhūtiśakti which is the material cause of the world, च्रेअतिओन् of the world takes place (ch. 5-7).
The created world which in the beginning is under the influence of सत्त्व, goes on smoothly for some time. As सत्त्व diminishes increasing the influence of रजस् and तमस्, people start going astray necessitating the proclamation of the original Śāstra (holy book) viz., the Pāñcarātra, by सङ्कर्षण himself (an aspect of Lord वासुदेव). The book describes the four aspects of manifestation of the Supreme Lord: पर, vyūha, विभव and arca. (See PĀÑCARĀTRA ĀGAMA for details.)
Then follow the descriptions of philosophical systems like Trayī, Sāṅkhya and योग ending with the सात्वत (Pāñca-rātra). It is interesting to note that बुद्धिस्म् and जैनिस्म् are dismissed as śāstrābhāsa (fallacious systems) invented by gods and ṛṣis to spread confusion among the wicked!
The summum bonum of life is ‘atyanta हित’ (‘greatest well-being’) which puts a permanent end to all suffering and gives eternal bliss. This can be gained by धर्म (religion) and ज्ञान (knowledge), the former being the stepping stone for the latter. Both these are described in the Pāñcarātra system, by following which मोक्ष (liberation) can be gained.
Then there is a detailed description of mantras (sacred syllables), characteris-tics of the आचार्य (preceptor), शिष्य (disciple) and दीक्षा (initiation). (vide chapters 18 to 20.)
Rakṣās and yantras (magical diagrams), their worship and meditation as also the fruits accruing from them are described next (chs. 21 to 29). Practice of योग is also dealt with in detail (chs. 30, 31). Astras or magical weapons are another topic described in detail.
Human beings naturally desire cures from all physical and mental diseases. This subject also has been dealt with. The cures suggested are ritualistic or mystical. There is also a detailed description of the महाभिषेक (‘great baptism’) by the performance of which one can get rid of all diseases (ch. 39).
There are a number of upākhyānas (stories) given to illustrate the effects of divine weapons and of certain amulets and talismans.
The great Sudarśanamantra, the root of all mantras, which enables one to cause the सुदर्शन पुरुष to appear before oneself, is another subject dealt with (chs. 43, 44).
Other mantras described in the work are: tārāmantra (i.e. Om), mantras of विष्णु and नारायण, meaning of the word namaḥ, नरसिṁह-मन्त्र, गायत्री, explanation of some sections of Puruṣa-सूक्त, Śrīsūkta and others.
Unlike the Vaikhānasa works, this work of the Pāñcarātra system does not deal with temples and rituals.

ahiṁsā
(‘non-violence’)
------------------------------------------
Ahimsā or non-violence has been a highly extolled virtue throughout Indian history. In fact, it is as old as the Ṛgveda itself. To quote one मन्त्र: mā vo ghnataṁ mā śapatam prati voce deva yantam, ‘Return not blow for blow, nor curse for curse, neither meanness for base tricks. Shower blessings instead’ (Ṛgveda Saṁhitā 4.1.8). Even during the Vedic period, when अनिमल् सच्रिड़िचेस् existed and the animals were believed to attain हेअवेन्, the animal meant for immolation was made unconscious before being killed, so that it did not suffer. Prayers were offered and expiations done to ward off the effects of the sin of killing the animal which was inevitable in the sacrifices (vide Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.7.9.8).
Coming to the उपनिषद्स्, the earliest reference to अहिṁसा as an ethical discipline is found in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (3.17.4; 8.15.1) where it has been bracketed with truth. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (5.2.3) emphasises the need for cultivating compassion, the corollary of अहिṁसा. The Mahābhārata often calls it the highest धर्म (ahiṁsā paramo dharmaḥ—1.11.13-14). The पुराणस् and धर्म-śāstras extol it in glowing terms. It is even termed as ‘sanātanadharma’ (the ancient religion) by some पुराणस् like the Brahmāṇda and Matsya, and also des-cribed as the gateway to धर्म. The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (2.30) lists it as the first virtue to be cultivated by the aspirant for योग.
Ahiṁsā is not injuring other living beings in thought, word and deed. This is the ideal to be relentlessly pursued by those who have dedicated their lives to the realization of the आत्मन् (the Self). For them it is a महाव्रत (great vow). Others should practise it as far as possible.
That physical injury or harsh words inflict pain and suffering is easily understood. However, what is not so easily understood is that inimical thoughts that one harbours against others harm both. This is a fact—whether one concedes it or not—as all minds, being parts of the one चोस्मिच् मिन्द्, are interconnected, so that a thought arising in one मिन्द् concerning another मिन्द् can always cause a reaction in the other, good for good and bad for bad.
Ahiṁsā can never be practised perfectly without its complement, love. They are two sides of the same coin. Anyone who has practised it effectively radiates a wonderful atmosphere of peace. Even animals with mutual and natural enmity, if they come within the orbit of this influence, live in peace and harmony (vide Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि 2.35).
Some of the पुराणस् (vide—Brahmāṇḍa 2. 36. 188) recommended the killing of tyrants and desperados and opined that such killing is no हिṁसा at all, since many will live in happiness and peace by their death.
Buddhism and जैनिस्म् have accorded अहिṁसा the topmost place among virtues to be cultivated. जैनिस्म् has carried it to rather extreme lengths.

Ahīna
(‘lasting for several days’)
------------------------------------------
Sacrifices are considered to be the links between men and gods like इन्द्र. अहीन is one of the several kinds which come under the सोम group of sacrifices. It is a general nomenclature for all सोम sacrifices wherein the extraction of the सोम juice is spread over several days. Hence the name ‘Ahīna,’ ‘that which takes several days to perform’.
An अहीन is always begun on a full-मोओन् day. The extraction of सोम juice may be spread over 2 to 12 days. It should always end with an अतिरात्र (another सोम sacrifice spread over a day and night). Along with the दीक्षा (consecration of the sacrificer at the beginning) and upasad (another small sacrifice of the इष्टि type) the whole sacrifice should not extend beyond a month.
The well-known अश्वमेध sacrifice belongs to the अहीन group.
See also ATIRĀTRA and DĪKṢĀ.

āhitāgni
(‘One who has laid the sacrificial fire’)
------------------------------------------
One who has established the Vedic fires by performing the अग्न्याधान ceremony is called an आहिताग्नि. According to जैमिनि’s Pūrva Mīmāṁsā Sūtras, an आहिताग्नि has to maintain the fires and utensils throughout his life. On his death, he is cremated in his fire along with the sacrificial utensils which are placed on the different parts of his body. This is called pratipatti. (vide Śābarabhāṣya on 11.3.34)
See also AGNYĀDHĀNA.
